name: Annualised volatility
brief:
Volatility is how widely returns spread around their average. Desks quote it per year so that a daily series and a weekly one can be compared.

Write `annualised_vol(prices, periods=252)`. It takes closing prices in time order and returns the annualised volatility of their simple returns. There are 252 trading days in a year.
definition:
With $n$ simple returns $r_1, \dots, r_n$ and their mean $\bar r$, the sample standard deviation is

$$s = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{t=1}^{n} (r_t - \bar r)^2}$$

The annualised volatility is $s \sqrt{k}$, where $k$ is `periods`. Return `0.0` when there are fewer than two returns.
constraints: Use the sample standard deviation, dividing by $n - 1$, as pandas does by default.
Standard library only. NumPy and pandas are not loaded. `statistics` and `math` are fine.
All tests share a 5-second time limit.
hint: Build the returns first. Then the mean, then the sum of squared deviations divided by one fewer than the number of returns. Take the square root and multiply by `math.sqrt(periods)`.

tests.name: Empty list
tests.why: With no prices there is no spread to measure. Return `0.0`.

tests.name: One return
tests.why: One return has no spread: the sample standard deviation needs at least two. Return `0.0`.

tests.name: Steady growth
tests.why: Both returns are 0.1, so they do not spread at all and the volatility is 0.

tests.name: Sample, not population
tests.why: Divide the squared deviations by $n - 1$, not $n$. With two returns the gap is a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

tests.name: Square root of time
tests.why: Variance grows with time, so volatility scales by $\sqrt{252}$, not by 252.

tests.name: Weekly prices
tests.why: Use the `periods` you are given. Weekly data has 52 periods a year.

tests.name: No annualising
tests.why: With `periods=1` the answer is the plain sample standard deviation of the returns.

tests.name: Daily closes
tests.why: Use simple returns, $P_t / P_{t-1} - 1$, then the sample standard deviation, then scale.

tests.name: Long series
tests.note: 50,000 prices from a seeded random walk
tests.why: This test has 50,000 prices. One pass for the mean and one for the deviations is enough.

how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests, from an empty list to 50,000 prices. A float counts when it is within a relative 1e-9 of the expected value, or within 1e-12 of it near zero.
where: Part of the 1.1 exit project: returns, annualised volatility and maximum drawdown from a CSV of daily prices.
notes: Dividing by `n - 1` gives the sample variance, which pandas `.std()` uses by default.
Volatility scales with the square root of time because variances of independent returns add.
`statistics.stdev(rets)` computes the same $s$, if you prefer the library.
prelude:
def _walk(n, seed, start, step):
    # Seeded random walk from an integer LCG, so every Python makes the same prices
    x = seed
    p = start
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) % 2147483648
        p = p * (1 + step * ((x % 2001 - 1000) / 1000))
        out.append(p)
    return out
